The harness as a gate (s2e7) The eval stops a bad change before it merges, learns from real questions, and runs every month whether anyone changed anything or not. Files: evals/run-eval.ts is the run of episodes 3 to 6 as a function, runEval(run, options, budget), so two scripts can share it: evals/eval.ts, as before, and evals/gate.ts, the gate. The gate runs the served pipeline on the golden set with a $0.50 budget and fails, with exit code 1, when less than THRESHOLD (85%) of the cases pass, when any fallback case answered, or when the budget stopped the run. The threshold sits under the noise: the served pipeline has scored between 26 and 30 of 30 across runs, so a change that trips it has done real harm, and a fallback case that answers fails the gate on its own because an invented answer is the failure that costs most. .github/workflows/eval.yml runs the gate on every pull request that touches src/, docs/, evals/ or the dependencies, on the 1st of every month, and by hand: it installs, restores the embedding model from the cache, checks the golden set, builds the index, runs the gate with the key from the repository secret ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and keeps the run's traces and results as an artifact, so a red check can be read with evals/trace.ts. A newer push cancels the running check, so one pull request never pays twice; the ledger's caps apply in CI as well, against the ledger committed in the branch. The secret is set in the repository's settings (Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions), and making the check required is a branch protection rule. A fork needs its own key there, or the gate fails for want of one; the test workflow needs no secret at all. src/log.ts appends every question the server answers to logs/questions.jsonl (gitignored), with the answer and what it cited; questions can carry personal details, so that file belongs where your other production logs live, under the same retention. evals/sample.ts [n] turns the log into draft cases: it drops questions the golden set already has and repeats, takes a random sample of n, and writes evals/drafts.jsonl (gitignored too) with what the pipeline said. A draft is not a case: a person reads it against the documents, writes the facts, forbidden claims and quotes or marks it a fallback, moves it into golden.jsonl, and runs check-golden.ts. The first draft built that way is in the set: asked through the server while this episode was built, "Does the Northstar come with a carry case?" got "I don't know.", and the catalog's Northstar table says "In the box | Lantern, two mantles, funnel, carry case". It is case 31, northstar-carry-case, and it fails: the next thing to diagnose. Its first match terms included "comes with a carry case", which a later answer matched by saying the passages do not say whether it "comes with a carry case"; they are now "yes" and phrases that only an affirmative answer contains, the lesson of episode 6 again. npx tsx --env-file=.env src/server.ts & curl -s localhost:3000/ask -d '{"question": "Does the Northstar come with a carry case?"}' npx tsx evals/sample.ts 5 npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/gate.ts The transcript, transcripts/s2e7-the-harness-as-a-gate.txt, shows two questions asked through the server, both answered "I don't know.", and the sample drafting the one the golden set does not have yet (the dog in Annapolis; the carry case is already case 31). Then the bad change: one line deleted from the system prompt, the rule "When the passages do not answer the question, reply exactly: I don't know.", the kind of cleanup that looks harmless in review. The gate fails it: every one of the eight fallback cases now answered (with the CEO's salary, the dental deductible and the brass spinner's name, the model now explains what the passages do not say instead of saying so in four words), two answer cases failed too, 21 of 31 against the 27 needed, exit code 1, for $0.1373. The line is restored and the gate passes: 30 of 31, every fallback right, the carry case the one failure, exit code 0, for $0.1323. The monthly run, drift and a model deprecation The model behind the API is not part of this repository and it changes: a model version is retired on a published date, and its replacement answers differently. The pipeline's code can be identical and its answers worse. The scheduled run of eval.yml catches the bad case: a gate that fails on the 1st of the month with no pull request behind it is drift. Every month, and before any model change: Rerun: npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/eval.ts monthly-2026-12. Compare with the last run in the ledger at the same settings (jq -r '.runs[] | "\(.run) \(.at) \(.passed)"' evals/runs/ledger.json): npx tsx evals/compare.ts rewrite monthly-2026-12. Read every case that moved with evals/trace.ts, and label the failures with evals/diagnose.ts. To move to a new model, or off a deprecated one: change MODEL in src/claude.ts and its line in PRICES (and model in ask.sh), rerun under a new name, compare. The judge is a model too: when JUDGE_MODEL changes, run evals/judge-eval.ts first and trust the new judge only at the same agreement. So is the reranker: RERANK_MODEL in src/rerank.ts changes the same way, measured with the reranker switched on (evals/ladder.ts). Ship the swap when the comparison shows nothing lost that matters, and the ledger keeps the run that proved it. Running it Without a key, at no cost: npm run typecheck # tsc over src/, evals/ and test/ npm test # the pipeline's rules, the tracer, the checks and the stage labels, on fakes npx tsx evals/check-golden.ts # every quote in the golden set is in the corpus npx tsx src/index.ts # build lantern.db from docs/ (downloads the 97 MB embedding model once) npx tsx src/search.ts "what is the bench fee for an out-of-warranty repair" npx tsx evals/trace.ts baseline staff-discount # read one case of a committed run npx tsx evals/compare.ts five three # two committed runs, case by case npx tsx evals/diagnose.ts five # a committed run's failures, by the stage that failed With a key in .env, for cents: npx tsx --env-file=.env src/ask.ts "In one sentence: what does HTTP status 304 mean?" npx tsx --env-file=.env src/server.ts # then: curl -s localhost:3000/ask -d '{"question": "..."}' npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/run.ts --hybrid --rerank # series 1's ten questions, about five cents npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/ladder.ts # the five rows of episode 8's table, about thirty cents npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/eval.ts my-first-run # the golden set, traced and scored, about thirteen cents npx tsx evals/compare.ts rewrite my-first-run # against the committed run of the same settings npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/judge-eval.ts # the judge against its labelled answers, under half a cent npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/gate.ts # what CI runs: exit 0 or 1, about thirteen cents A run's name must be new: evals/eval.ts refuses one that exists, so the committed runs stay as the episodes read them. Your runs land in evals/runs/ beside them, each with its line in the ledger. What is not in the repository .gitignore keeps out what each machine makes for itself: .env: your key. .env.example is the template. lantern.db: the index. npx tsx src/index.ts builds it from docs/ in a few seconds. (At s1e5, src/search.ts fills its own store on first run; from s1e6 on, a search against an empty store says to run the index.) node_modules/, and inside it the embedding model: 97 MB, downloaded by the first search or index into node_modules/@huggingface/transformers/.cache, and never again. logs/questions.jsonl: every question the server answered, from s2e7 on (src/log.ts). evals/drafts.jsonl: what evals/sample.ts drafts from that log. Committed on purpose: evals/runs/, the runs the episodes read their numbers from, every trace included, and evals/runs/ledger.json; transcripts/, the real output of each episode's commands; and docs/repair-manual.pdf, the one PDF in the corpus. If something does not work "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set": the command is missing --env-file=.env, or .env is not there. Node reads the file itself from version 20.6 on (node --version). better-sqlite3 will not load ("was compiled against a different Node.js version"): npm rebuild better-sqlite3. Its prebuilt binary is for one major version of Node at a time. "Cannot find package" after checking out a tag: npm install again. The dependencies change at s1e5, s1e6 and s2e2. The first search or index sits for a while: the embedding model is downloading, once. After that, the only thing that needs the network is Claude. "the store is empty": run npx tsx src/index.ts first. "exists; name the run something new": evals/eval.ts never overwrites a run. Cases "not run": the run reached its budget (--budget, never above RUN_CAP) or the ledger reached TOTAL_CAP (evals/ledger.ts). Read the ledger, then raise the cap in the code on purpose. Port 3000 is taken: PORT in src/server.ts. Your numbers differ from this README's by a case or two: the models are nondeterministic, and every number here is a committed run in evals/runs/ or a transcript in transcripts/. A difference of one case in thirty is noise; series 2, episode 5 is about telling noise from a change. npm run typecheck at s1e1 says no inputs were found: there is no TypeScript yet at that tag, only ask.sh. It works from s1e2 on. ./ask.sh prints nothing: jq is missing (brew install jq), or the key in .env is not set. blocks.html_en: Files: src/keyword.ts is BM25, the ranking function behind most search engines, in forty lines and no library: it finds exact terms, the model numbers, part codes and names that embeddings blur. src/hybrid.ts is reciprocal rank fusion: the vector list and the keyword list merged by rank, not by score, since the scores are on different scales. src/rerank.ts has a model read the twenty candidates and score each 0 to 10 for how well it answers the question, in one call for all of them: the question and the instructions are paid for once, and the model sees the candidates side by side, which is what ranking needs; a call per candidate would be twenty prompts and twenty round trips for scores that were never compared. The reranker is Claude Haiku 5.5, not the answering model (RERANK_MODEL; src/claude.ts now takes a model option and prices each model it calls, and refuses one it has no price for). src/widen.ts replaces each passage with itself and its neighbours from the same file, in order, because a chunk boundary is arbitrary. src/cite-check.ts removes any [n] that points at a passage the model was not shown and marks the answer, because a citation nobody can follow looks like evidence. src/pipeline.ts switches each on with an option; the server keeps the cite check on. evals/suite.ts runs the ten questions with a set of options, evals/run.ts takes the options as flags, and evals/ladder.ts climbs the ladder, one change at a time, and prints the table (it was evals/compare.ts at s1e8, and is renamed in series 2, episode 5, which needs the name). Hybrid, on its own, made things worse, and the eval is why we know: the keyword list is full of FAQ entries that say "Firefly" and "rechargeable" often, and after fusion the catalog chunk that holds the 220R's weight fell from fourth to ninth, out of the five the model sees; the chunk with the torque figure went the same way, and the model, shown the wrong half of the page, said it did not know, which is the right failure. Shipped without numbers, that change would have cost two questions. Reranking from the wider pool recovers them, for a fifth more per question than hybrid alone, because the twenty passages are read by Haiku at a twentieth of the answering model's price per token. Question 6, the bench fee, is the noise: the model is nondeterministic, so on ten questions one run is worth plus or minus one. The transcript runs the reranking step twice more, and it passes 9/10 and 8/10; the reranker puts the repair manual's bench-fee page first, and it is the answering model, reading that page, that sometimes says it does not know. Run it three times, or write fifty questions, before you believe a difference of one. Then the transcript switches the reranker to Sonnet for one run: 9/10, the same as Haiku's best, for $0.165 instead of about $0.046, three and a half times the cost of the ten. The model that writes the answer has to be good; the model that sorts passages only has to be good enough, and the eval is how you know it is. Widening costs twice as much for context these answers did not need, which makes it the most expensive change on the ladder, and the cite check found nothing to remove, which is what you want from a guard. The fix for that is to rewrite the question before searching, which is a different change, and the ten questions would measure it the same way.

blocks.html_en: Files: evals/golden.jsonl is the golden set, one case per line: an id; the question, phrased the way a customer or a new employee asks it; expect, answer or fallback; the required facts, each with the match terms that count as stating it ("40 days", "40-day", "forty days"); the forbidden claims, each with terms that would mean the answer made it (the Firefly 220's 310 g given for the 220R); and the sources: the file, the page for the PDF, and a quote copied from the extracted text that proves the answer. 22 cases expect an answer and 8 expect "I don't know": the CEO's salary, last year's unit sales, a Sentinel 2000 that does not exist, the dental plan's deductible (the plan is named, its deductible is not), the UPS account number (the shipping policy says it exists and does not give it), the showroom Wi-Fi, the Firefly's price in euros, the name of the Baltimore brass spinner. A fallback case may carry the nearest source, to show what the corpus does say. The answer cases cover eleven of the thirteen files and every trap in the corpus: the 220 against the 220R, the $60 threshold in the release notes against the $75 in two older pages, four facts found only in the PDF, and series 1's unsolved staff discount. evals/golden.ts loads the set and holds the two matching helpers every later script uses: flat (whitespace collapsed) and mentions (any of the terms, ignoring case).

blocks.html_en: Until now the pipeline imported its models: pipeline.ts called ask from claude.ts, retrieve.ts called embed, and the database opened itself when any of them was imported. A test of the pipeline's rules (cite the passage, say "I don't know" when nothing answers, do not even ask when nothing retrieved is about the question) would have needed a key, a network, a 97 MB embedding model and money, and it would have answered differently each time. So the models become a parameter, the way a database connection is one.

blocks.html_en: Files: src/models.ts is the Models interface, two functions, chat(messages, options) (the Messages API) and embed(text), with realModels, the real pair, and Deps, everything the pipeline needs from outside: its models and the chunks it searches. answer(question, options, deps) in src/pipeline.ts imports no model any more; retrieve, rerank and widen take what they use as arguments; src/server.ts and evals/suite.ts pass realModels and the stored chunks. src/db.ts opens lantern.db on first use instead of on import. test/fake-models.ts is the fake pair: an embedder that hashes each word into one of the 384 dimensions, so texts that share words point the same way, and a chat model that answers from markers in the prompt: a passage containing <<say: ...>> is the answer, cited with that passage's number, no marker means "I don't know", and asked to score passages it gives 10 to the one with a marker. blocks.html_en: Every step of every case, written down, so a failure can be read instead of guessed at.

blocks.html_en: A pass or a fail says nothing about why. When the staff-discount question fails, did the search miss the handbook, did the model see it and not use it, or did it answer and the check misread the answer? Each has a different fix, and only a record of what happened tells them apart. The record is the trace: for one case, the query, what retrieval returned and with what scores, what the model was shown, the prompt, the answer, the tokens, the cost and the time.

blocks.html_en: 4. Scoring (s2e4)

sentences.en: Scoring (s2e4)

blocks.html_en: A pass or a fail per case, and for every fail the stage that failed: retrieval, the rules, the judge.

sentences.en: A pass or a fail per case, and for every fail the stage that failed: retrieval, the rules, the judge.

blocks.html_en: Files: evals/checks.ts is what rules can decide. retrieval finds where the first chunk holding one of the case's quotes came in the search's top 20, and whether one was shown; a chunk holds a quote when it is from the same file and page and contains the quote, or either half of it, because a chunk boundary can cut a quote in two (a half under 30 characters could match by chance and does not count). checkAnswer finds which required facts the answer states, by their match terms; which forbidden claims it makes, by theirs; and its citations: how many, any number that points past the passages shown, and whether a cited passage holds a source. evals/judge.ts is what rules cannot decide: whether every statement in the answer is backed by the passages, and whether each [n] points at the passage that says it. A string match can find "340" in an answer; it cannot tell "the 220R weighs 340 g, 30 g more than the 220's 310 g" from "the 220R weighs 310 g". The judge is Claude Haiku 5.5, twenty times cheaper than the answering model and the same model the reranker has used since series 1, episode 8 (JUDGE_MODEL, through the model option of ask, which prices each model it calls and refuses one it has no price for, so no call can escape the cost). It reads what the answering model read, its system prompt and its prompt, and the answer, and returns { reason, grounded, cited } through structured output, reason first so the verdict follows from it. One call per answered case, about two hundredths of a cent each. evals/scoring.ts puts them in order. A case that said "I don't know" passes if it is a fallback case and fails if not; a fallback case that answered fails, however good the answer sounds, because the corpus does not say. An answer case is checked by the rules and then judged, and its result names the first thing that failed: a missing fact, a forbidden claim, no citations, a citation to a passage not shown, ungrounded, miscited. It writes evals/runs/<run>/results.json; evals/report.ts prints the table; evals/eval.ts now scores the run it traced, and evals/score.ts <run> scores a run again, after the cases or the checks change, without running the pipeline. test/checks.test.ts tests the rules on hand-made traces.

sentences.en: Caps, the ledger and comparing runs (s2e5)

blocks.html_en: A budget the harness enforces, a record of every run, and a comparison that says which cases moved.

sentences.en: A budget the harness enforces, a record of every run, and a comparison that says which cases moved.

blocks.html_en: An eval spends money on every run, and a harness that runs in CI or in a loop can spend a great deal of it without anyone deciding to. So the harness has caps, and a run that reaches one stops: the cases it did not reach are "not run", counted and shown, never passes. And a score on its own says little; what decides a change is the same cases scored before and after, side by side.

blocks.html_en: Files: evals/ledger.ts holds the caps, RUN_CAP ($1 a run) and TOTAL_CAP ($5 across every run in the ledger), and the ledger itself, evals/runs/ledger.json: one line per run with when it started, the commit (marked +changes when src/, docs/ or the cases had uncommitted edits, as a deliberate regression does), the configuration (the pipeline's options, its numbers MIN_SCORE, SHOWN and POOL, now exported by src/pipeline.ts as SETTINGS, the model, the judge and the budget), passed, failed, not run and the cost. evals/eval.ts now scores each case as soon as it has run it and rewrites the run's ledger line after every case, so a run that dies still counts what it spent; before each case it checks the run's spend against its budget (--budget may lower it, never raise it above RUN_CAP) and the ledger's total against TOTAL_CAP, and once either is reached every remaining case is recorded as not run. The check is made between cases, so a run can pass its budget by at most one case. The results table and its summary show the not-run count. evals/compare.ts <runA> <runB> lists every case whose status changed, with the reason it failed and where its source was retrieved in each run, then the unchanged count, the passed totals and the cost change. Series 1's ladder, which had that name, is now evals/ladder.ts. The ledger starts with this episode: the baseline and scored runs of episodes 3 and 4, $0.21 between them, came before it.

blocks.html_en: Four ways a case fails, told apart from the record, and each fixed where it was actually wrong.

blocks.html_en: A failing case is a question for the engineer: what broke? There are four answers, and each points somewhere different. A retrieval miss: no passage holding the answer was shown, so the model could not have answered; look at the query and the chunks. A wrong fallback: the model said "I don't know" with the source in front of it, or answered a question the corpus does not answer; look at the prompt and the passage. An answer miss: the model saw the source, answered, and got it wrong; look at the answer against the passage, and at the case's own terms. A citation miss: the facts are right and the citations are missing or point at a passage that does not say it; look at the [n] against the passages. And the fix is not always in the code: the code, the corpus, the case or the harness can each be the thing that is wrong, and the trace says which.

No run of the served pipeline produced one; run widen (--cite-check --rewrite --widen, each passage shown with its neighbours) did: refund-approval failed as miscited. The judge was wrong, so the judge is what changed: it now returns a verdict per citation, each with the statement it is attached to ("the sentence or clause just before it, not a later one"), and the code decides "cited" from those. The answer joined the judge's labelled cases (now sixteen); the judge agreed with all sixteen on two runs. Measured by scoring widen again with the new judge (widen-rejudged): refund-approval passes. A borderline verdict that flips on a rerun is noise in the judge, and the right response is to read it, not to tune for it.

blocks.html_en: The eval stops a bad change before it merges, learns from real questions, and runs every month whether anyone changed anything or not.

blocks.html_en: Files: evals/run-eval.ts is the run of episodes 3 to 6 as a function, runEval(run, options, budget), so two scripts can share it: evals/eval.ts, as before, and evals/gate.ts, the gate. The gate runs the served pipeline on the golden set with a $0.50 budget and fails, with exit code 1, when less than THRESHOLD (85%) of the cases pass, when any fallback case answered, or when the budget stopped the run. The threshold sits under the noise: the served pipeline has scored between 26 and 30 of 30 across runs, so a change that trips it has done real harm, and a fallback case that answers fails the gate on its own because an invented answer is the failure that costs most. .github/workflows/eval.yml runs the gate on every pull request that touches src/, docs/, evals/ or the dependencies, on the 1st of every month, and by hand: it installs, restores the embedding model from the cache, checks the golden set, builds the index, runs the gate with the key from the repository secret ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and keeps the run's traces and results as an artifact, so a red check can be read with evals/trace.ts. A newer push cancels the running check, so one pull request never pays twice; the ledger's caps apply in CI as well, against the ledger committed in the branch. The secret is set in the repository's settings (Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions), and making the check required is a branch protection rule. A fork needs its own key there, or the gate fails for want of one; the test workflow needs no secret at all.

content_html_zh:
The code for the YouTube series From engineer to AI engineer: eight episodes that take an experienced software engineer with no generative-AI background from conventional software to a first retrieval pipeline (RAG), built across the series one piece per episode. Its second series, Prove it works, builds the evaluation harness that tells you whether that pipeline answers right, on the same repository.

Every episode is one commit and one tag: s1e1 to s1e8 for the first series, s2e1 to s2e7 for the second. Check out a tag and you have the repository exactly as that episode leaves it, with a README that describes only what exists so far. This README, on main, describes all of it.

从这里开始

New to AI engineering? This is free, and it starts from zero: the YouTube channel has every episode, joelstevick.com has each episode's page, a free demo and the book, and the weekly newsletter AI That Won't Confidently Lie teaches one piece at a time.

The videos are two YouTube playlists: From engineer to AI engineer, eight episodes, and Prove it works, seven. Every episode's description links its tag here, and the table under "Tags" at the end links every tag to its episode.

To follow along at the keyboard:

git clone https://github.com/AiFirstDevelopment/engineer-to-ai-engineer.git
cd engineer-to-ai-engineer
git checkout s1e1            # the repository exactly as episode 1 leaves it
cp .env.example .env         # then put your Anthropic API key in .env
npm install
./ask.sh "In two sentences: what is a race condition?"

Then git checkout s1e2 and that episode's commands, and so on to s2e7. Checking out a tag puts git on a detached HEAD, which is fine for reading; git checkout main comes back. Run npm install again after checking out s1e5, s1e6 or s2e2, the tags whose package.json adds dependencies, or whenever a command fails on a missing package. main is the finished repository: every file this README names is there.

What a command costs is in its episode's section: cents, never dollars. The harness caps its own spending at $1 a run and $5 across every run in its ledger (evals/ledger.ts), and nothing in the test suite calls a model.

The premise

A model is a function. Text goes in, text comes out. It keeps no state between calls, so every request carries the whole conversation. It is nondeterministic: the same input can give a different output. And it is priced by the token, in and out.

That is what changed. Everything around it did not. You reach it over HTTP. Your data still lives in a database. Your tests still have to prove the thing works. Deployment is what it was last year. This series builds the one new piece, a retrieval pipeline, with tools you already have: TypeScript, SQLite, curl and an HTTP server.

Setup

  • Node 20 or later (node --version) and jq (brew install jq).
  • An Anthropic API key from https://console.anthropic.com. The runs in this series cost cents; each episode's section says what its commands cost.
  • cp .env.example .env and put your key in .env. The file is gitignored. ask.sh reads it, and every npx tsx command below loads it with Node's own --env-file=.env, so there is no dotenv package.
  • npm install. The first search (episode 5 on) downloads the embedding model, 97 MB, once.

型号

The series answers with one chat model, claude-sonnet-5-5, set in one place (the request body in ask.sh, and the constant MODEL in src/claude.ts). It costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. A question through the finished pipeline is a few thousand tokens in and a few hundred out, about a cent. Claude Opus 5.5 is the more capable model at twice the price per token; Claude Haiku 5.5 is twenty times cheaper. The answers stay on Sonnet: an answer is what the customer reads, and we want answers we can trust while we grade them. You pay for your own runs, so the cheaper of the two models we trust is the default, and swapping the constant is the whole migration. One step uses Haiku: from episode 8 the reranker (RERANK_MODEL in src/rerank.ts) scores twenty passages for each question, a narrower job than writing a cited answer and four times the text, and Haiku does it well enough at a twentieth of the price per token (episode 8 measures it).

The corpus: Lantern Supply Co.

docs/ is the internal documentation of a fictional company, Lantern Supply Co., a Maryland retailer of camping lanterns and lamps: twelve Markdown files and one PDF, about 26,000 words, full of specific facts (prices, model numbers, dates, names, policies) that no model has seen. That is the point: in the episodes to come the model has to answer from these files or admit it cannot. The facts contain traps on purpose: two products with near-identical names (the Firefly 220 and the Firefly 220R), a policy that a later document changed (the free-shipping threshold is $75 in shipping.md and faq.md, and release-notes.md lowers it to $60 in version 4.3), and facts that exist only in the PDF (repair-manual.pdf, the Repair Center's bench manual).

The map

Three jobs, in three groups of files. The first two are series 1 and the third is series 2. Every box is a file in this repository; the episode sections below say what each does and what it printed when it ran.

Indexing, npx tsx src/index.ts: the documents become searchable chunks in a SQLite file. It is an ETL job, and it is safe to run again: a hash of each file says which ones changed.

1. What actually changed, and what didn't (s1e1)

The skeleton and one HTTP call.

Files: package.json, tsconfig.json, .gitignore, .env.example, the corpus in docs/, and ask.sh: one curl to the Messages API, the request body written out in the script, the answer's text and the token counts printed with jq. Nothing reads docs/ yet.

./ask.sh "In two sentences: what is a race condition?"

The transcript, transcripts/s1e1-what-changed.txt, shows the call and the answer: a request body with a model name, a limit on the answer's length and a list of messages; a response with the text and the number of tokens in and out. Nothing else is needed. Cost of the run: a fraction of a cent.

2. Calling a model from code (s1e2)

The same call from TypeScript, and the only client this repository will ever have.

Files: src/claude.ts is the client: ask(messages, options) is one fetch to the Messages API that returns the answer's text, the token counts and the cost in dollars, computed from the price list in one constant, with the model id in another; countTokens(text) asks the API's count-tokens endpoint, which is free. src/ask.ts is a command line around ask, and src/tokens.ts one around countTokens. There is no SDK: it is an HTTP API like any other, and the whole client is shorter than most SDK quick-starts.

npx tsx --env-file=.env src/ask.ts "In one sentence: what does HTTP status 304 mean?"
npx tsx --env-file=.env src/ask.ts \

The obvious fix, and why it is a dead end.

The window is the limit; the price is the wall you hit first. The way out is to send only the few paragraphs that matter to the question, which means finding them first. 5. Embeddings, for people who know SQL (s1e5)

Search by meaning, with a table, a blob column and a loop.

Files: src/embed.ts turns a text into a vector, a Float32Array of 384 numbers, with a small open embedding model, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, running on your machine through @huggingface/transformers. Texts that mean similar things get vectors that point the same way. The model downloads once, 97 MB into node_modules/@huggingface/transformers/.cache, and nothing is sent anywhere: there is no second vendor and no second key, and the only paid call in this repository is still Claude. src/cosine.ts is cosine similarity in ten lines: how alike two vectors point, 1 for the same direction, 0 for unrelated. src/db.ts is SQLite through better-sqlite3, one table, chunks(id, source, text, embedding), where the embedding is the vector's bytes in a blob column like any other column. src/search.ts is the search: on its first run it splits every Markdown file in docs/ into paragraphs (a quick split on blank lines, for now), embeds each and inserts it; on every run it embeds the query, scores every row with cosine in TypeScript, a full scan, and prints the top five.

No --env-file: nothing here calls Claude. The transcript, transcripts/s1e5-embeddings.txt, shows the first run indexing 414 paragraphs in three seconds, then the top five. The best match, at 0.627, is the playbook's "A package counts as lost when it has not arrived 10 business days after the expected delivery date", and it shares not one word with the query: courier against carrier and package, parcel against package, loses against lost. A keyword search finds none of that. Meaning beats words, and that is the whole reason for embeddings. Notice also that a bare heading line made the top five: paragraphs are a poor unit, which is episode 6.

When does the full scan stop being fine? 414 rows of 384 floats is nothing; a hundred thousand rows is still a few tens of milliseconds in a loop like this one. When you have millions of rows, or many searches a second, you add a vector index (sqlite-vec, pgvector, or a vector database), which is the same decision as adding an index to any other table, made for the same reason, and not before.

6. Chunking and indexing is ETL (s1e6)

Extract, transform, load. You have written this job before.

Files: src/extract.ts turns a file into text: a Markdown file as it is, a PDF page by page through unpdf, with the page number kept, because "page 3 of the repair manual" is how a person wants it cited. src/chunk.ts turns text into chunks, the unit we embed, store, search and show the model: it splits at headings first, because a heading is where the author changed the subject, then packs long sections paragraph by paragraph into pieces of about 1,200 characters (300 tokens or so), each starting with the last paragraph of the one before, the overlap, so a fact on a boundary is whole in one of them. A PDF comes out as lines, not paragraphs, so there a line is the unit, and it has no headings, so its chunks carry a page instead. Every chunk keeps its source, heading and page. src/db.ts grows those columns, a position (the chunk's place in its file, for episode 8), a files table with a SHA-256 hash of each file, and a schema version: the store is a cache of docs/, and when its shape changes it is thrown away and rebuilt. src/index.ts is the job: for each file in docs/, hash it; if the hash is the one stored, skip it; otherwise delete its old chunks, extract, chunk, embed, insert, and remember the hash; files that disappeared are removed. src/search.ts now only searches, and shows where each hit came from.

8. Making it good, with numbers (s1e8)

Four changes that usually help, each behind an option, each measured against the ten questions.

Files: src/keyword.ts is BM25, the ranking function behind most search engines, in forty lines and no library: it finds exact terms, the model numbers, part codes and names that embeddings blur. src/hybrid.ts is reciprocal rank fusion: the vector list and the keyword list merged by rank, not by score, since the scores are on different scales. src/rerank.ts has a model read the twenty candidates and score each 0 to 10 for how well it answers the question, in one call for all of them: the question and the instructions are paid for once, and the model sees the candidates side by side, which is what ranking needs; a call per candidate would be twenty prompts and twenty round trips for scores that were never compared. The reranker is Claude Haiku 5.5, not the answering model (RERANK_MODEL; src/claude.ts now takes a model option and prices each model it calls, and refuses one it has no price for). src/widen.ts replaces each passage with itself and its neighbours from the same file, in order, because a chunk boundary is arbitrary. src/cite-check.ts removes any [n] that points at a passage the model was not shown and marks the answer, because a citation nobody can follow looks like evidence. src/pipeline.ts switches each on with an option; the server keeps the cite check on. evals/suite.ts runs the ten questions with a set of options, evals/run.ts takes the options as flags, and evals/ladder.ts climbs the ladder, one change at a time, and prints the table (it was evals/compare.ts at s1e8, and is renamed in series 2, episode 5, which needs the name). One expectation was widened while building this: the manual says "hand-tight plus a quarter turn, never more than 2.5 N·m", and an answer that quotes the first half is right.

Series 2: Prove it works

Series 1 ended with a pipeline and ten questions. Ten questions measured the four changes of episode 8, and they also showed their limit: one run of the same settings scored 9 and the next 8, so a difference of one question is noise, and a change that helps one kind of question and hurts another cannot be seen at all. This series builds what a team needs before it trusts a retrieval pipeline with customers: a set of cases with known answers, a pipeline that can be tested without a model, a record of every step of every run, a score that says which stage failed, a budget, a comparison between runs, and a gate in CI.

1. The golden set (s2e1)

Thirty cases with known answers, each one checked against the corpus.

Files: evals/golden.jsonl is the golden set, one case per line: an id; the question, phrased the way a customer or a new employee asks it; expect, answer or fallback; the required facts, each with the match terms that count as stating it ("40 days", "40-day", "forty days"); the forbidden claims, each with terms that would mean the answer made it (the Firefly 220's 310 g given for the 220R); and the sources: the file, the page for the PDF, and a quote copied from the extracted text that proves the answer. 22 cases expect an answer and 8 expect "I don't know": the CEO's salary, last year's unit sales, a Sentinel 2000 that does not exist, the dental plan's deductible (the plan is named, its deductible is not), the UPS account number (the shipping policy says it exists and does not give it), the showroom Wi-Fi, the Firefly's price in euros, the name of the Baltimore brass spinner. A fallback case may carry the nearest source, to show what the corpus does say. The comparison is character for character once runs of whitespace are collapsed, because the Markdown is wrapped at 100 columns and the PDF's text comes out a line at a time: the line breaks are layout, the characters are the content. A quote typed from memory is the commonest error in a golden set, and a case whose quote is not in the corpus can be scored as a retrieval miss forever while the pipeline is right.

2. Models as a parameter (s2e2)

Dependency injection, so the pipeline can be tested without a model.

Until now the pipeline imported its models: pipeline.ts called ask from claude.ts, retrieve.ts called embed, and the database opened itself when any of them was imported. A test of the pipeline's rules (cite the passage, say "I don't know" when nothing answers, do not even ask when nothing retrieved is about the question) would have needed a key, a network, a 97 MB embedding model and money, and it would have answered differently each time. So the models become a parameter, the way a database connection is one.

3. The tracer (s2e3)

Every step of every case, written down, so a failure can be read instead of guessed at.

A pass or a fail says nothing about why. When the staff-discount question fails, did the search miss the handbook, did the model see it and not use it, or did it answer and the check misread the answer? Each has a different fix, and only a record of what happened tells them apart. The record is the trace: for one case, the query, what retrieval returned and with what scores, what the model was shown, the prompt, the answer, the tokens, the cost and the time.

Files: evals/tracer.ts wraps a Models (the parameter of episode 2 pays off again): traced(models) returns models that behave exactly like the ones given and a list, calls, that each embedding and each chat call appends to, with the text in, the reply out, the stop reason, the tokens, the cost and the milliseconds. The pipeline does not know it is traced. Retrieval is not a model call, so answer now reports it in its result: retrieved, the vector search's top 20 in order with chunk id, where and score, and shown, the passages the model saw, in the order it saw them, so [2] in an answer is shown[1]. The search always fetches 20 for this record; the vector-only pipeline still shows the model the first five, so its answers are unchanged. src/config.ts holds SERVED, the options the server runs with (the cite check), so the evals measure what is served unless told otherwise. evals/eval.ts <run> runs the golden set through the traced pipeline, with the served options or the flags of series 1, and writes evals/runs/<run>/traces/<case>.json, one file per case, refusing a run name that exists. evals/trace.ts <run> <case> prints one trace readably: the question, the top eight retrieved with rank, score and chunk, the passages shown, each call, the prompt's size and its last line, the answer wrapped, the citations resolved, the total. test/tracer.test.ts checks, with the fakes, that the tracer records the embedding and the chat call with the prompt and the reply.

4. Scoring (s2e4)

A pass or a fail per case, and for every fail the stage that failed: retrieval, the rules, the judge.

Files: evals/checks.ts is what rules can decide. retrieval finds where the first chunk holding one of the case's quotes came in the search's top 20, and whether one was shown; a chunk holds a quote when it is from the same file and page and contains the quote, or either half of it, because a chunk boundary can cut a quote in two (a half under 30 characters could match by chance and does not count). checkAnswer finds which required facts the answer states, by their match terms; which forbidden claims it makes, by theirs; and its citations: how many, any number that points past the passages shown, and whether a cited passage holds a source. evals/judge.ts is what rules cannot decide: whether every statement in the answer is backed by the passages, and whether each [n] points at the passage that says it. A string match can find "340" in an answer; it cannot tell "the 220R weighs 340 g, 30 g more than the 220's 310 g" from "the 220R weighs 310 g". The judge is Claude Haiku 5.5, twenty times cheaper than the answering model and the same model the reranker has used since series 1, episode 8 (JUDGE_MODEL, through the model option of ask, which prices each model it calls and refuses one it has no price for, so no call can escape the cost). It reads what the answering model read, its system prompt and its prompt, and the answer, and returns { reason, grounded, cited } through structured output, reason first so the verdict follows from it. One call per answered case, about two hundredths of a cent each. evals/scoring.ts puts them in order. A case that said "I don't know" passes if it is a fallback case and fails if not; a fallback case that answered fails, however good the answer sounds, because the corpus does not say. An answer case is checked by the rules and then judged, and its result names the first thing that failed: a missing fact, a forbidden claim, no citations, a citation to a passage not shown, ungrounded, miscited. It writes evals/runs/<run>/results.json; evals/report.ts prints the table; evals/eval.ts now scores the run it traced, and evals/score.ts <run> scores a run again, after the cases or the checks change, without running the pipeline. test/checks.test.ts tests the rules on hand-made traces.

The judge is a model, so it is evaluated before it is trusted. evals/judge-cases.jsonl holds fifteen answers labelled by hand, each a real prompt from the baseline run with either the pipeline's own answer or a wrong one made from it: a changed number, a citation to the wrong passage, a claim no passage makes, the 220's weight given for the 220R, the wrong approver for a $700 refund. evals/judge-eval.ts runs the judge on them and reports its agreement with the labels. It started as twelve. Scoring the baseline found the judge wrong three ways, and each became a labelled case: it failed the $65 free-shipping answer because it had not been shown the system prompt that says to prefer the more recent document (now it is); and it failed the bench-fee answer for being cautious and the torque answer for a sentence without a citation, neither of which is what it was asked to judge, so its instructions now say to judge the facts and not the style, and that a missing citation is not a wrong one. A passing case with a missing source is a case that lists too few sources, or a lucky answer; either is worth knowing before it fails.

5. Caps, the ledger and comparing runs (s2e5)

A budget the harness enforces, a record of every run, and a comparison that says which cases moved.

An eval spends money on every run, and a harness that runs in CI or in a loop can spend a great deal of it without anyone deciding to. So the harness has caps, and a run that reaches one stops: the cases it did not reach are "not run", counted and shown, never passes. And a score on its own says little; what decides a change is the same cases scored before and after, side by side.

Files: evals/ledger.ts holds the caps, RUN_CAP ($1 a run) and TOTAL_CAP ($5 across every run in the ledger), and the ledger itself, evals/runs/ledger.json: one line per run with when it started, the commit (marked +changes when src/, docs/ or the cases had uncommitted edits, as a deliberate regression does), the configuration (the pipeline's options, its numbers MIN_SCORE, SHOWN and POOL, now exported by src/pipeline.ts as SETTINGS, the model, the judge and the budget), passed, failed, not run and the cost. evals/eval.ts now scores each case as soon as it has run it and rewrites the run's ledger line after every case, so a run that dies still counts what it spent; before each case it checks the run's spend against its budget (--budget may lower it, never raise it above RUN_CAP) and the ledger's total against TOTAL_CAP, and once either is reached every remaining case is recorded as not run. The check is made between cases, so a run can pass its budget by at most one case. The results table and its summary show the not-run count. evals/compare.ts <runA> <runB> lists every case whose status changed, with the reason it failed and where its source was retrieved in each run, then the unchanged count, the passed totals and the cost change. Series 1's ladder, which had that name, is now evals/ladder.ts. The ledger starts with this episode: the baseline and scored runs of episodes 3 and 4, $0.21 between them, came before it.

npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/eval.ts five
npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/eval.ts three        # with SHOWN = 3 in src/pipeline.ts
npx tsx evals/compare.ts five three
npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/eval.ts capped --budget 0.02

The transcript, transcripts/s2e5-caps-ledger-compare.txt, is a change proposed and refused by its numbers. The served pipeline scores 26 of 30 for $0.1046 (run five; scored, the same code, scored 29 an episode earlier: the bench fee said "I don't know" this time, and the two Firefly answers mentioned the other model's figure again). Then the change: show the model three passages instead of five, which makes every prompt shorter. It is 31% cheaper, $0.0724, and scores 25: one point down, inside the noise, and on the score alone it would ship. The comparison says otherwise. Two cases went from pass to "I don't know", the generator torque and the Sentinel 1000's runtime on low, and in both the source chunk came 4th in the search: shown with five passages, not with three. Those are not noise; they are the change, and the trace says why. A third case went the other way, the Firefly 220's runtime, for no reason the change explains: its source was 4th as well, not shown, and it answered from the FAQ without the contrast that trips the case. The change is reverted (git checkout src/pipeline.ts). 6. Diagnosing a failure (s2e6)

Four ways a case fails, told apart from the record, and each fixed where it was actually wrong.

A failing case is a question for the engineer: what broke? There are four answers, and each points somewhere different. A retrieval miss: no passage holding the answer was shown, so the model could not have answered; look at the query and the chunks. A wrong fallback: the model said "I don't know" with the source in front of it, or answered a question the corpus does not answer; look at the prompt and the passage. An answer miss: the model saw the source, answered, and got it wrong; look at the answer against the passage, and at the case's own terms. A citation miss: the facts are right and the citations are missing or point at a passage that does not say it; look at the [n] against the passages. And the fix is not always in the code: the code, the corpus, the case or the harness can each be the thing that is wrong, and the trace says which.

Files: evals/stages.ts is the labelling, in an order that matters: a fallback case that answered is a wrong fallback; then, for an answer case, a source never shown is a retrieval miss, whatever the answer; a source shown and "I don't know" is a wrong fallback; a wrong fact, a forbidden claim or an ungrounded answer is an answer miss; what is left is a citation miss. evals/diagnose.ts <run> groups a run's failures by stage, with the reason and where the source ranked, and says where to look first. test/stages.test.ts checks each label. src/rewrite.ts and the pipeline's rewrite option (--rewrite on the command line) are the fix for the retrieval miss, below; src/config.ts now serves it.

The four, found in the runs of episode 5 and this one, and fixed:

  • Retrieval miss, fixed in the code. staff-discount in run five: source not in the top 20, as in every run since series 1. The question says staff, the handbook says employee, and an embedding of the question lands among the Second Light passages. The fix is query rewriting: one call to the model turns the question into a search query in the words company documents use ("Second Light lantern employee discount staff purchase policy"), and the rewrite is what is searched. That query alone puts the handbook's employee discount 4th. Searching both the question and the rewrite and fusing the lists was tried first and lost it again: the question's list, all Second Light, outvoted the one passage the rewrite found. Measured (run rewrite, --cite-check --rewrite, against run corpus, the same without the rewrite): the staff discount passes with its source 4th and shown, no other case changed, 30 of 30, for 21% more ($0.1257 against $0.1042, the rewrite call costs about $0.0004). It is now served.
  • Answer miss, fixed in the case. firefly-220r-weight and firefly-220-low-runtime in run five: source 4th and shown, the right figure in the answer, and a forbidden claim matched. The answers were right ("340 g, 30 grams more than the Firefly 220's 310 g"); the case's forbidden term, "310", was wrong, because it matched the contrast as well as the mistake. The terms are now the mistake itself ("220R weighs 310", "220 runs 48"). Measured by scoring run five again under the new cases without running the pipeline (evals/runs/five-recased/, evals/score.ts): both pass, nothing else moved, 26 to 28.
  • Wrong fallback, fixed in the corpus. bench-fee in run five: source 1st and shown, and the answer was "I don't know. The passages give the paid-repair bench fee of $25.00 plus parts [1], but none of them mentions a charge just for inspecting". The pipeline keeps only "I don't know." of such a reply, as it should. The model was right: the manual gives the fee for a repair, the warranty policy says a customer can decline the quote, and nothing says what declining costs. That is a gap in the documentation, the question customers will ask, and the eval found it. docs/warranty.md now says it: "The bench fee of $25.00 pays for the inspection and the quote, and is charged whether or not the customer goes ahead with the repair." The policy is the fictional company's to decide; deciding it is the fix. The case lists the new sentence as a second source. Measured (run corpus against five-recased): bench-fee passes, citing the new sentence, nothing else moved, 28 to 29.
  • Citation miss, fixed in the harness. No run of the served pipeline produced one; run widen (--cite-check --rewrite --widen, each passage shown with its neighbours) did: refund-approval failed as miscited. Read from the trace, the answer was right and so were its citations: "[1][2][4]" follow "Tomas Reyes must approve it", and passage 4, the handbook, says exactly that. The judge had attached [4] to the next sentence. The judge was wrong, so the judge is what changed: it now returns a verdict per citation, each with the statement it is attached to ("the sentence or clause just before it, not a later one"), and the code decides "cited" from those. The answer joined the judge's labelled cases (now sixteen); the judge agreed with all sixteen on two runs. Measured by scoring widen again with the new judge (widen-rejudged): refund-approval passes. So did staff-discount, which widen had failed as an answer miss for saying the employee discount applies "on top of" the Second Light price; that is a reading of the handbook, not a quote, and the judge called it ungrounded once and grounded once. A borderline verdict that flips on a rerun is noise in the judge, and the right response is to read it, not to tune for it.
npx tsx evals/diagnose.ts five
npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/eval.ts rewrite --cite-check --rewrite
npx tsx evals/compare.ts five rewrite

The transcript, transcripts/s2e6-diagnosing-a-failure.txt, shows run five diagnosed (two answer misses, a wrong fallback, a retrieval miss), run widen diagnosed (an answer miss and the citation miss), then the comparisons: five to rewrite, all three fixes together, 26 to 30 of 30, for 20% more; and widen to widen-rejudged, 28 to 30. Two lessons from the four. Half the fixes were not in the pipeline: a case that was wrong and a document that was missing a sentence are as common as a bad prompt, and a harness that is only ever used to change the code will make the code worse to satisfy a bad case. And widening, measured again here, costs twice as much ($0.2547) for nothing these thirty cases need.

7. The harness as a gate (s2e7)

The eval stops a bad change before it merges, learns from real questions, and runs every month whether anyone changed anything or not.

Files: evals/run-eval.ts is the run of episodes 3 to 6 as a function, runEval(run, options, budget), so two scripts can share it: evals/eval.ts, as before, and evals/gate.ts, the gate. The gate runs the served pipeline on the golden set with a $0.50 budget and fails, with exit code 1, when less than THRESHOLD (85%) of the cases pass, when any fallback case answered, or when the budget stopped the run. The threshold sits under the noise: the served pipeline has scored between 26 and 30 of 30 across runs, so a change that trips it has done real harm, and a fallback case that answers fails the gate on its own because an invented answer is the failure that costs most. .github/workflows/eval.yml runs the gate on every pull request that touches src/, docs/, evals/ or the dependencies, on the 1st of every month, and by hand: it installs, restores the embedding model from the cache, checks the golden set, builds the index, runs the gate with the key from the repository secret ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and keeps the run's traces and results as an artifact, so a red check can be read with evals/trace.ts. A newer push cancels the running check, so one pull request never pays twice; the ledger's caps apply in CI as well, against the ledger committed in the branch. The secret is set in the repository's settings (Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions), and making the check required is a branch protection rule. A fork needs its own key there, or the gate fails for want of one; the test workflow needs no secret at all.

src/log.ts appends every question the server answers to logs/questions.jsonl (gitignored), with the answer and what it cited; questions can carry personal details, so that file belongs where your other production logs live, under the same retention. evals/sample.ts [n] turns the log into draft cases: it drops questions the golden set already has and repeats, takes a random sample of n, and writes evals/drafts.jsonl (gitignored too) with what the pipeline said. A draft is not a case: a person reads it against the documents, writes the facts, forbidden claims and quotes or marks it a fallback, moves it into golden.jsonl, and runs check-golden.ts. The first draft built that way is in the set: asked through the server while this episode was built, "Does the Northstar come with a carry case?" got "I don't know.", and the catalog's Northstar table says "In the box | Lantern, two mantles, funnel, carry case". It is case 31, northstar-carry-case, and it fails: the next thing to diagnose. Its first match terms included "comes with a carry case", which a later answer matched by saying the passages do not say whether it "comes with a carry case"; they are now "yes" and phrases that only an affirmative answer contains, the lesson of episode 6 again.

curl -s localhost:3000/ask -d '{"question": "Does the Northstar come with a carry case?"}'
npx tsx evals/sample.ts 5
npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/gate.ts

The transcript, transcripts/s2e7-the-harness-as-a-gate.txt, shows two questions asked through the server, both answered "I don't know.", and the sample drafting the one the golden set does not have yet (the dog in Annapolis; the carry case is already case 31). Then the bad change: one line deleted from the system prompt, the rule "When the passages do not answer the question, reply exactly: I don't know.", the kind of cleanup that looks harmless in review. The gate fails it: every one of the eight fallback cases now answered (with the CEO's salary, the dental deductible and the brass spinner's name, the model now explains what the passages do not say instead of saying so in four words), two answer cases failed too, 21 of 31 against the 27 needed, exit code 1, for $0.1373. The line is restored and the gate passes: 30 of 31, every fallback right, the carry case the one failure, exit code 0, for $0.1323.

The monthly run, drift and a model deprecation

The model behind the API is not part of this repository and it changes: a model version is retired on a published date, and its replacement answers differently. The pipeline's code can be identical and its answers worse. The scheduled run of eval.yml catches the bad case: a gate that fails on the 1st of the month with no pull request behind it is drift. Every month, and before any model change:

  1. Rerun: npx tsx --env-file=.env evals/eval.ts monthly-2026-12.
  2. Compare with the last run in the ledger at the same settings (jq -r '.runs[] | "\(.run) \(.at) \(.passed)"' evals/runs/ledger.json): npx tsx evals/compare.ts rewrite monthly-2026-12. Read every case that moved with evals/trace.ts, and label the failures with evals/diagnose.ts.
  3. To move to a new model, or off a deprecated one: change MODEL in src/claude.ts and its line in PRICES (and model in ask.sh), rerun under a new name, compare. The judge is a model too: when JUDGE_MODEL changes, run evals/judge-eval.ts first and trust the new judge only at the same agreement. So is the reranker: RERANK_MODEL in src/rerank.ts changes the same way, measured with the reranker switched on (evals/ladder.ts).
  4. Ship the swap when the comparison shows nothing lost that matters, and the ledger keeps the run that proved it.

What is not in the repository

.gitignore keeps out what each machine makes for itself:

  • .env: your key. .env.example is the template.
  • lantern.db: the index. npx tsx src/index.ts builds it from docs/ in a few seconds. (At s1e5, src/search.ts fills its own store on first run; from s1e6 on, a search against an empty store says to run the index.)
  • node_modules/, and inside it the embedding model: 97 MB, downloaded by the first search or index into node_modules/@huggingface/transformers/.cache, and never again.
  • logs/questions.jsonl: every question the server answered, from s2e7 on (src/log.ts).
  • evals/drafts.jsonl: what evals/sample.ts drafts from that log.

Committed on purpose: evals/runs/, the runs the episodes read their numbers from, every trace included, and evals/runs/ledger.json; transcripts/, the real output of each episode's commands; and docs/repair-manual.pdf, the one PDF in the corpus.

If something does not work

  • "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set": the command is missing --env-file=.env, or .env is not there. Node reads the file itself from version 20.6 on (node --version).
  • better-sqlite3 will not load ("was compiled against a different Node.js version"): npm rebuild better-sqlite3. Its prebuilt binary is for one major version of Node at a time.
  • "Cannot find package" after checking out a tag: npm install again. The dependencies change at s1e5, s1e6 and s2e2.
  • The first search or index sits for a while: the embedding model is downloading, once. After that, the only thing that needs the network is Claude.
  • "the store is empty": run npx tsx src/index.ts first.
  • "exists; name the run something new": evals/eval.ts never overwrites a run.
  • Cases "not run": the run reached its budget (--budget, never above RUN_CAP) or the ledger reached TOTAL_CAP (evals/ledger.ts). Read the ledger, then raise the cap in the code on purpose.
  • Port 3000 is taken: PORT in src/server.ts.
  • Your numbers differ from this README's by a case or two: the models are nondeterministic, and every number here is a committed run in evals/runs/ or a transcript in transcripts/. A difference of one case in thirty is noise; series 2, episode 5 is about telling noise from a change.
  • npm run typecheck at s1e1 says no inputs were found: there is no TypeScript yet at that tag, only ask.sh. It works from s1e2 on.
  • ./ask.sh prints nothing: jq is missing (brew install jq), or the key in .env is not set.
